n: This chapter, often called the Table of Nations, maps how Noah’s descendants spread into peoples around the ancient world. It shows that every nation shares one family origin.

f.g: Hebrew toledot — family history; a section marker in Genesis.

n: Japheth’s sons are listed first. Many of these names match peoples north and west of Israel, such as the Medes (Madai) and Greeks (Javan).

f.g: The Ionians or Greeks.
The Medes of ancient Iran.

n: Gomer’s descendants probably settled around the Black Sea and Asia Minor (modern Turkey).

f.g: Probably a people of eastern Asia Minor (compare Ezekiel 27:14).
A northern people; later Jewish tradition used the name for Germany.

n: Javan’s descendants are seafaring peoples of the Mediterranean, including Cyprus (Kittim) and perhaps Spain (Tarshish).

f.g: A distant port, possibly in Spain; Jonah later tried to flee there (Jonah 1:3).
Cyprus, and later used for western peoples generally.

n: These coastland peoples spread out, each with its own language and land. The phrase “after his tongue” anticipates the scattering of languages at Babel in chapter 11.

f.g: Coastlands and islands, especially around the Mediterranean.
Here simply “nations.”

n: Ham’s sons are linked with lands to the south and in Canaan: Cush (Nubia), Mizraim (Egypt), Phut (probably Libya), and Canaan.

f.g: The Hebrew name for Egypt.
The region south of Egypt (Nubia/Sudan).

n: Cush’s descendants are linked with Arabia and East Africa, such as Sheba, famous later for its queen who visited Solomon.

f.g: A trading people of northwestern Arabia.

n: Nimrod is introduced as the first great “mighty one”—a warrior and empire-builder.

f.g: A powerful warrior or tyrant; the same word (gibbor) used of the men of renown in 6:4.

n: Nimrod becomes proverbial as a mighty hunter. “Before the LORD” may mean “in God’s sight” or even “in defiance of God”; later Jewish tradition remembered him as rebellious.

f.g: Can mean “in the sight of” or “against” the Lord.

n: Nimrod’s kingdom begins in famous Mesopotamian cities like Babel (Babylon), Erech (Uruk), and Accad. This sets the stage for the tower of Babel in chapter 11.

f.g: Babylon, which becomes a symbol of worldly pride throughout scripture.
Southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq).

n: From there, power extends north into Assyria and its great cities, including Nineveh. Assyria later conquers the northern kingdom of Israel.

f.g: Assyria; the phrase may also mean Nimrod “went out into Assyria.”

n: Resen lies between Nineveh and Calah, together forming a great urban region.

f.g: Later known as Nimrud, a major Assyrian capital.

n: Egypt’s descendants are listed by peoples, most of whom are now hard to identify.

f.g: Probably a North African people.

n: Among Egypt’s offshoots are the Philistines, Israel’s later rivals, connected here with Caphtor, probably Crete.

f.g: The Philistines.
People of Caphtor, likely Crete.

n: Canaan’s sons include Sidon, a major Phoenician city, and Heth, ancestor of the Hittites. Abraham will later buy a burial place from the sons of Heth.

f.g: A major Phoenician port city on the coast of modern Lebanon.

n: These are peoples Israel will encounter in the promised land, such as the Jebusites of Jerusalem and the Amorites.

f.g: The inhabitants of Jerusalem before David captured it.

n: More Canaanite peoples are named, some linked with cities on the coast of Syria and Lebanon.
The Canaanite families spread through the land.

f.g: People of Hamath, a city in Syria.

n: The borders of Canaan are traced from Sidon to Gaza and to the cities near the Dead Sea, including Sodom and Gomorrah. This is the land later promised to Abraham.

f.g: Location unknown, probably near the Dead Sea.

n: A summary closes Ham’s line: families, languages, lands, and nations.

f.g: By their languages.

n: Shem is introduced as the ancestor of “all the children of Eber.” From Eber’s name comes the word “Hebrew,” so Shem’s line leads to Abraham and Israel.

f.g: Likely the source of the word “Hebrew.”

f.w: the brother of Japheth the elder
f.g: Can mean either Shem or Japheth was the elder; the Hebrew is ambiguous.

n: Shem’s sons include peoples to the east and north: Elam (in Iran), Asshur (Assyria), and Aram (Syria). Arphaxad leads to Abraham.

f.g: The Arameans of Syria; Abraham’s relatives later live there (Genesis 24:10).

n: Aram’s sons include Uz, a name also given to Job’s homeland.
The line runs from Arphaxad to Salah to Eber, the ancestor of the Hebrews.
In Peleg’s day “the earth was divided.” Peleg means “division.” This may refer to the scattering at Babel; some Latter-day Saints have also connected it with a division of land masses.

f.g: Means “division.”

n: Joktan’s sons are listed. Many seem to be tribes of the Arabian Peninsula, such as Hazarmaveth (Hadramaut in Yemen).

f.g: Likely the Hadramaut region of southern Arabia.

n: More of Joktan’s descendants, likely Arabian tribes.

f.g: Possibly an old name for Sanaa in Yemen.

n: Joktan’s line also includes another Sheba, showing the name was shared by more than one people.

f.g: A southern Arabian kingdom; compare the Cushite Sheba in verse 7.

n: Ophir becomes famous for fine gold in Solomon’s day.
Joktan’s families settle across a region “of the east,” likely in Arabia.

f.g: Eastern hill country; exact locations are uncertain.

n: A summary closes Shem’s line.

f.g: Organized by family, language, land, and nation.

n: The chapter ends by stating that all nations came from Noah’s sons. The Bible’s story is ultimately about one human family, which God will bless through Abraham.

f.w: by these were the nations divided
